title: Design Council, The Double Diamond
text:
## The Double Diamond design process

The Double Diamond is a visual representation of the design and innovation process. It is a simple way to describe the steps taken in any design and innovation project, regardless of the methods and tools used. First articulated by the UK Design Council in 2005, it has become one of the most widely used maps of the design process.

## The two diamonds

The model has two diamonds. Each diamond represents a process of exploring an issue more widely or deeply (divergent thinking) and then taking focused action (convergent thinking). Each diamond widens as the team opens up to many possibilities, then narrows as the team makes decisions and commits. The first diamond is about designing the right thing (understanding and defining the problem). The second diamond is about designing the thing right (developing and delivering the solution).

## The four phases

Discover: the first diamond helps people understand, rather than simply assume, what the problem is. It involves speaking to and spending time with people who are affected by the issues. This is the research and empathy phase.

Define: the insight gathered from the discovery phase can help you to define the challenge in a different way. Teams reframe the problem, converging on a clear, actionable problem statement or design brief.

Develop: the second diamond encourages people to give different answers to the clearly defined problem, seeking inspiration from elsewhere and co-designing with a range of different people. This is where ideation, sketching, and prototyping of multiple solutions happen.

Deliver: delivery involves testing out different solutions at small scale, rejecting those that will not work and improving the ones that will. Solutions are refined and made ready to launch.

## Design principles and mindset

The Design Council pairs the process with a set of design principles for the people who use it: be people-centred (start with the people using a service or product), communicate visually and inclusively (help people gain a shared understanding), collaborate and co-create (work together and get inspired by what others are doing), and iterate (spot errors early, avoid risk, and build confidence in your ideas). A core insight is that it is common to loop back and repeat phases as understanding deepens; the diamonds are not a strictly linear one-way street. As IDEO's Tim Brown framed the spirit of it, the Double Diamond is not an instruction manual on how to design, it is an invitation to get involved. The Design Council later expanded the model into its Framework for Innovation, adding the ideas that organisations may return to earlier phases as new problems emerge and that in digital contexts ideas are never truly finished.

title: Brad Frost, Atomic Design (Chapter 2: Atomic Design Methodology)
text:
## Atomic Design methodology

Atomic Design is a methodology composed of five distinct stages working together to create interface design systems in a more deliberate and hierarchical manner. The five stages are atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages. Atomic design is not a linear process, but rather a mental model to help us think of our user interfaces as both a cohesive whole and a collection of parts at the same time. The stages borrow from chemistry: atoms combine to form molecules, which combine into organisms, which are assembled into templates and finally pages.

## Atoms

Atoms are the basic building blocks of matter. Applied to web interfaces, atoms are the basic HTML elements like form labels, inputs, buttons, and others that cannot be broken down any further without ceasing to be functional. Atoms include more abstract elements like color palettes, fonts, and animations. Each atom has its own unique properties, for example a specific font size or color value, which affect how it is applied across the system. Atoms on their own are not terribly useful, but they are good for reference in a pattern library because you can see all your global styles laid out at a glance.

## Molecules

Molecules are relatively simple groups of UI elements functioning together as a unit. For example, a form label, a search input, and a button can join together to create a search form molecule. Composed of atoms, molecules are the backbone of design systems. The classic single responsibility principle applies: giving a molecule one clearly defined job encourages reusability, consistency, and testability. When you build simple components that do one thing well, the whole system becomes more maintainable.

## Organisms

Organisms are relatively complex UI components composed of groups of molecules and/or atoms and/or other organisms. Organisms form distinct sections of an interface. A header organism, for instance, might combine a logo atom, a primary navigation molecule, and a search form molecule. Building from molecules to organisms encourages creating standalone, portable, reusable components. Organisms can consist of similar or different molecule types, and they give us a sense of the interface coming to life.

## Templates

Templates are page-level objects that place components into a layout and articulate the design's underlying content structure. Templates are where we begin to see the design coming together and demonstrate how the components look and function together. Crucially, templates focus on the page's underlying content structure rather than the final content itself. They articulate content parameters such as image sizes and the character length of headings and text passages, defining the skeleton so real content can flow in.

## Pages

Pages are specific instances of templates that show what a UI looks like with real representative content in place. Pages are the highest level of fidelity and, because they are the most tangible, they are typically where the most attention is paid and stakeholders sign off. Pages are essential for testing the effectiveness of the underlying design system. By seeing everything in place with real content, you can loop back to modify your molecules, organisms, and templates to better address the real, tangible content variations. It is important to test how resilient the design is when, for example, a user enters a very long name or a section holds far more content than the average case.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, UX Prototypes: Low Fidelity vs. High Fidelity
text:
## What prototype fidelity means

Fidelity refers to how closely a prototype matches the look and feel of the final product. Prototypes can be low-fidelity or high-fidelity, and fidelity is not a single dial but varies across several independent dimensions. A prototype can be high fidelity in one dimension and low fidelity in another, so a designer should deliberately choose the level of fidelity for each dimension based on what they need to learn.

## The dimensions of fidelity

Visual fidelity concerns details of the visual design: colors, sizes, spacing, graphics, and layout. Low visual fidelity uses hand-drawn sketches, wireframes, or schematic blocks; high visual fidelity uses realistic, detailed visuals matching the final look.

Content fidelity concerns the actual content shown. Low content fidelity uses placeholder text such as Lorem Ipsum or greeked content and summary stand-ins; high content fidelity uses real or realistic content, full articles, actual product descriptions, and real images.

Interactivity (functional) fidelity concerns how much the user can actually do. In a fully functional high-fidelity prototype the user can click through and the prototype responds; in low interactivity, a person may play computer and manually swap screens, or interaction may be limited to a few hotspots.

## When to use low fidelity

Low-fidelity prototypes are faster and cheaper to create, so more of the design effort can go into iterating before testing. They are easier to change mid-test, they put less pressure on test participants who feel freer to criticize rough work, and designers stay less emotionally invested in throwaway sketches. Stakeholders can clearly see that the work is not finished, which keeps feedback focused on structure and flow rather than pixels.

## When to use high fidelity

High-fidelity prototypes let you test realistic system response, specific UI components, affordances, and micro-interactions. Users behave more realistically and treat the prototype like live software, which surfaces genuine reactions. High fidelity frees the facilitator to observe rather than operate the prototype and minimizes human error during testing. The tradeoff is time and cost, and the risk that people fixate on visual polish or become reluctant to suggest large changes to something that looks finished.

## The decision

Choose low fidelity when you want speed and rapid iteration on structure, flow, and concept. Choose high fidelity when you need to evaluate specific interactions, visual design, or realistic workflows where system realism matters. Match the fidelity of each dimension to the specific question you are trying to answer.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, The Role of Design Critiques
text:
## What a design critique is

A design critique is the process of analyzing a design and giving feedback on whether it meets its objectives. It is a group conversation aimed at improving the work, not a judgment and not an approval gate. Critiques are most valuable when they are cross-disciplinary, bringing multiple perspectives to bear on whether the design solves the right problem for the right people.

## Critique versus design review

A standalone critique is different from a design review. A standalone critique focuses solely on improving a specific piece of work and can happen at any point. A design review evaluates a design against heuristics and usually happens at the end of a process for approval purposes. Conflating the two, treating a critique as a sign-off meeting, undermines the open, exploratory tone that makes critique useful.

## Roles

Two primary roles exist. The presenter shares the work and its context. The critiquer offers perspectives and feedback. Multiple people can occupy each role, and a facilitator often runs the session.

## Three foundational principles

Clear scope prevents unwieldy conversations with ambiguous boundaries; the group should know exactly what is and is not up for discussion. Agreed-upon design objectives establish a common understanding of the problem and user needs; without shared objectives, feedback collapses into subjective opinion. Conversation rather than command: critique should foster open discussion, and directive comments (telling the designer what to do) undermine its purpose.

## Best practices for presenters

Reiterate the objectives and personas before beginning. Tell a story that explains the context and the decision points that led to the design. Present efficiently and avoid over-explaining or getting defensive about details. Where possible, distribute the work beforehand so critiquers respond thoughtfully rather than with reactive gut responses.

## Facilitation approaches

Round robin has participants share sequentially, ensuring everyone contributes rather than letting the loudest voice dominate. Quotas ask each critiquer for a set number of positive and negative observations to seed balanced discussion. The facilitator creates and distributes the scope and agenda, reformulates opinionated or directive comments so they relate back to the design goals, documents the discussion publicly, and follows up with a summary and action items.

## Anti-patterns

Common critique failures include not establishing personas or objectives beforehand, scheduling excessively long sessions, taking feedback personally, rushing to solve the problem during the critique instead of surfacing issues, and focusing exclusively on negatives. The recommended way to build the habit is to start soon and start small, for example a 30-minute weekly session on current work, before expanding scope and inviting cross-department participants.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Gestalt Principles of Visual Perception in UI
text:
## Gestalt principles in visual design

The Gestalt principles are principles that explain how humans simplify and organize complex images that consist of many elements, by subconsciously arranging the parts into an organized system that creates a whole. In interface design, applying these principles increases usability because it helps users understand the information architecture intuitively and see which elements belong together.

## Proximity

Proximity is the most important principle for user experience. Items positioned visually closer together are perceived as belonging to the same group. On a signup form, keeping each field label near its corresponding text box clarifies which information goes where. When spacing is inconsistent, for example on a crowded form, users become confused about which label is associated with which field. Proximity is often more powerful than borders or color for communicating grouping.

## Similarity

Elements that share visual characteristics such as color, shape, size, or orientation are grouped together mentally by users. Similarity lets you signal that separate items are related, or that a set of links behaves the same way, purely through consistent visual treatment.

## Common region

Elements placed inside the same visual container or boundary are understood as unified. A card with a background fill or an enclosing border creates a common region, grouping its contents even when they are not particularly close together.

## Continuation

Elements arranged on a line or a curve are perceived as more related than elements not on that path. The eye follows a continuous path, which is why aligned items read as a coherent group and why lists and rows feel connected.

## Closure

The brain fills in missing information to complete a recognizable shape. Logos such as the NBC peacock, or an illustration made of incomplete strokes, are perceived as whole figures even though the visual data is incomplete.

## Figure/ground

Users instinctively separate a focal element (the figure) from its surroundings (the ground). Clear figure/ground relationships, for example a modal dialog over a dimmed background, direct attention to what matters.

## Symmetry and order

Elements arranged in a balanced, orderly way are perceived as a cohesive, intentional whole. Symmetry and order convey stability and make interfaces feel trustworthy and easy to parse. Used together, these principles let a designer control grouping and attention with layout and spacing rather than heavy visual dividers.

title: Don Norman, The Design of Everyday Things (Revised Edition)
text:
## The fundamental principles of interaction

Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things sets out the fundamental principles of interaction that make products understandable and usable. The core concepts are affordances, signifiers, mapping, feedback, conceptual models, constraints, and discoverability. The revised edition notes that the underlying science is largely unchanged except for the important addition of the concept of signifiers, which sharpens the earlier idea of affordances.

## Affordances and signifiers

An affordance is a relationship between the properties of an object and the capabilities of the agent using it, that is, the possibilities for action that an object offers. A chair affords sitting; a flat plate on a door affords pushing. A signifier is a communicative cue that signals where an action should take place or what action is possible. Norman's key clarification is that affordances determine what actions are possible, while signifiers communicate where and how to take those actions. Good design makes affordances discoverable through clear signifiers; a door that must be pushed should not have a pull handle.

## Mapping

Mapping is the relationship between controls and their effects in the world. Good mapping exploits spatial correspondence and cultural conventions so that the layout of controls matches the layout of the things they control, for example stove burner knobs arranged to mirror the burners. Natural mapping reduces the need for labels, memory, and instruction.

## Feedback

Feedback is communicating the results of an action back to the user. Feedback must be immediate, informative, and matched to the action; too little feedback leaves users unsure whether anything happened, while too much feedback (a system that nags constantly) is ignored and becomes noise. Every action should produce a perceptible, appropriate response.

## Conceptual models and the system image

A conceptual model is a mental explanation of how something works. Users build conceptual models from the way a product presents itself, which Norman calls the system image, everything the user can perceive: the device, documentation, and behavior. When the system image is coherent, the user's conceptual model matches the designer's model and the product feels understandable. When it is not, users form wrong models and make errors.

## Constraints and discoverability

Constraints are limitations that guide behavior and reduce error. Norman identifies physical, cultural, semantic, and logical constraints; a good design uses constraints to make the wrong action difficult or impossible. Discoverability is the ability to figure out what actions are possible and how to perform them just by looking. Together with feedback, discoverability is what makes a product feel usable on first encounter.

## Human error and human-centered design

Norman argues that most problems blamed on human error are in fact bad design, captured in the phrase Human Error? No, Bad Design. He advocates human-centered design, an approach that puts human needs, capabilities, and behavior first and then designs to accommodate them. Design must also work across three levels of processing: visceral (immediate emotional response), behavioral (task performance and feel of use), and reflective (meaning, self-image, and long-term satisfaction). The book also describes the Seven Stages of Action, which trace how a person goes from a goal, through planning and executing an action, to perceiving and interpreting the result and evaluating it against the goal; the gulf of execution and the gulf of evaluation name the gaps a good design must bridge.

title: IDEO, Design Thinking (Desirability, Feasibility, Viability)
text:
## Design thinking at IDEO

IDEO defines design thinking as a human-centered approach to solving complex problems and to innovation. As Tim Brown, former IDEO CEO, put it: design thinking is a human-centered approach to innovation that draws from the designer's toolkit to integrate the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the requirements for business success.

## The three overlapping lenses

The defining idea is that good ideas live at the intersection of three considerations. Desirability asks what is desirable for people, what humans actually need and want. Feasibility asks what is technically and organizationally feasible with current or foreseeable technology. Viability asks what is financially viable and sustainable for the business. A solution that is desirable but not feasible or viable will not ship; one that is feasible and viable but not desirable will not be used. Design thinking works to find the sweet spot where all three overlap.

## Mindset over job title

IDEO frames design thinking not as becoming a designer but as adopting a problem-solving philosophy drawn from the mindset and craft of trained designers. It helps teams navigate uncertainty, generate new ideas, and learn by making and testing. It emphasizes working more creatively and collaboratively rather than defaulting to the first obvious answer.

## Process

Rather than a rigid recipe, IDEO describes design thinking as a flexible, iterative process. In its classic articulation the work moves through inspiration (understanding people and the problem), ideation (generating and refining many ideas), and implementation (bringing a solution to life). Learning by making, building rough prototypes early to think with your hands and to test ideas cheaply, is central. The process is meant to be looped through repeatedly, not walked once.

title: Design Tokens Community Group, Glossary
text:
## Design tokens: definitions from the standard

The Design Tokens Community Group (a W3C community group) maintains the shared vocabulary and format for design tokens across tools and platforms. The following are the core definitions.

## Design token

A design token is the single source of truth to name and store a design decision, distributed so teams can use it across design tools and coding languages. Tokens let a design decision, for example a brand color or a spacing unit, be defined once and consumed everywhere, keeping design and code in sync.

## Token name and value

A token name is a label assigned to a design decision; it is the identifier and should reflect purpose, for example text-color-primary or font-size-title. A token value is the context-specific value assigned to that name, such as a hex color, an RGB value, or a dimension in units like pixels or rem.

## Token types

Token types are predefined classifications that categorize token values. Tools use the type to determine a token's purpose and to enable format conversion. Documented examples of types include Color, Dimension, Duration, and Font family.

## Aliases and references

When a token's value references another token, it creates an alias. The referenced token becomes the authoritative value source, and changes propagate automatically to every token that depends on it. This is what enables tiered systems, for example a semantic token like background-color-disabled aliasing a raw palette token like color-neutral-20, so a single change ripples through the whole system.

## Composite tokens, files, and sets

Composite tokens combine multiple related style properties applied together, such as a typography token (font family, size, line height, color) or a shadow token (x and y offset, color, blur, spread). Token files are JSON documents (with .tokens or .tokens.json extensions) that contain tokens in the standardized format. Sets are collections of design tokens, containing inline declarations or references to external JSON files.

title: Nathan Curtis (EightShapes), Tokens in Design Systems
text:
## Tokens as decisions propagated through a system

Nathan Curtis of EightShapes frames design tokens as decisions propagated through a system. He distinguishes three levels. Options are the raw available choices, for example a hex code like #2B303B in a color palette. Decisions are options applied to a context, for example choosing a specific neutral to serve as a dark background. Tokens are those decisions propagated to any product, designer, or developer adopting the system. The value of a token is that it makes the decision visible and traceable wherever it is implemented, replacing buried hex codes and generic variables with intentional, purposeful names.

## Naming: option-level versus decision-level

Curtis shows the difference between option-level variables that describe appearance and decision-level tokens that describe intent. Option-level names look like $color-neutral-20, describing a value on a scale. Decision-level tokens look like $border-hairline, $background-color-light, $text-color-microcopy, and $background-color-disabled, describing where and why a value is used. Token names tend to follow patterns of category, concept, property, and variant. In his companion writing on naming, a fully namespaced token such as $esds-color-neutral-42 combines a namespace (esds for EightShapes Design System), a category (color), a concept or variant (neutral), and a scale value (42), all mapping to a concrete value like #6B6B6B.

## Ten tips to architect and implement tokens

Curtis offers practical guidance: show options before decisions so the system exposes both the palette and how it is applied; begin with color and typography and then expand to spacing, borders, motion, and beyond; use meaningful scales such as t-shirt sizing or numeric progressions rather than arbitrary values; invite contributions but designate a curator who guards coherence; graduate component-specific variables up into shared tokens once a pattern proves reusable; manage systemic change predictably by choosing the right level of token specificity; store tokens as reusable JSON so they are tool-agnostic; use human-readable formats like YAML for management; automate documentation directly from the token data; and embed token data into design tools so design and code draw from the same source of truth.

title: Interaction Design Foundation, Design Thinking (the five-stage d.school model)
text:
## Design thinking: a non-linear, iterative process

The Interaction Design Foundation describes design thinking as a non-linear, iterative process that teams use to understand users, challenge assumptions, redefine problems, and create innovative solutions. The most widely taught version is the five-stage model associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford (the d.school): Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test.

## Empathize: research users' needs

Teams conduct user-centric research to gain an empathic understanding of the people they are designing for. Through observation and user research, designers set aside their own assumptions and develop the best possible understanding of users, their needs, and their problems. Empathy is the foundation of human-centered design.

## Define: state users' needs and problems

Teams organize and analyze the observations gathered during empathy and synthesize them to define the core problems. The output is a problem statement framed from the user's perspective rather than the organization's objectives, for example a point-of-view statement that names a user, their need, and the insight behind it. Framing the right problem is what makes the later stages productive.

## Ideate: challenge assumptions and create ideas

With a clear problem statement, teams brainstorm alternative ways to view the problem and generate a large number of possible solutions. Ideation techniques (brainstorming, worst possible idea, and others) are used to push past obvious answers before converging and narrowing to the most promising options.

## Prototype: start creating solutions

Teams produce inexpensive, scaled-down versions of the product or of specific features to investigate the solutions generated. This is an experimental phase whose aim is to identify the best possible solution for each problem, learning cheaply what works and what does not before committing resources.

## Test: try solutions out

Teams test the prototypes with real users to evaluate whether they solve the problem. Testing often produces insights that redefine the problem or prompt a return to earlier stages. Crucially, the five stages are not always sequential; teams run them in parallel, out of order, and repeat them as needed, looping back whenever new understanding demands it.

title: Harry Brignull, Deceptive Design (Types of Deceptive Patterns)
text:
## Deceptive design patterns (anti-patterns)

Deceptive patterns, formerly called dark patterns, are tricks used in websites and apps that make users do things they did not mean to. Coined and catalogued by Harry Brignull, they are the canonical anti-patterns a product designer must recognize and refuse to build. Ethical product design means never manipulating users into decisions against their interest. The catalogue includes the following named types.

## The types

Forced action: the user wants to do something, but they are required to do something else undesirable in return. Sneaking: the user is drawn into a transaction on false pretences, because pertinent information is hidden or delayed. Hard to cancel: the user finds it easy to sign up or subscribe, but when they want to cancel they find it very hard. Preselection: the user is presented with a default option that has already been selected for them, in order to influence their decision-making. Obstruction: the user is faced with barriers or hurdles, making it hard for them to complete a task or access information. Hidden subscription: the user is unknowingly enrolled in a recurring subscription or payment plan without clear disclosure or explicit consent. Hidden costs: the user is enticed with a low advertised price, then after investing time and effort discovers unexpected fees and charges. Trick wording: the user is misled into taking an action due to confusing or misleading language. Visual interference: the user expects clear information, but it is hidden, obscured, or disguised. Fake social proof: the user is misled into believing a product is more popular or credible than it really is through fake reviews or testimonials. Fake urgency: the user is pressured into completing an action by a fake time limitation. Nagging: the user tries to do something but is persistently interrupted by requests to do something else. Confirmshaming: the user is emotionally manipulated into doing something they would not otherwise have done. Fake scarcity: the user is pressured by a fake indication of limited supply or popularity. Disguised ads: the user mistakenly believes they are clicking on an interface element or native content, but it is actually an advertisement. Comparison prevention: the user struggles to compare products because features and prices are combined complexly or essential information is hard to find. Addictive design: the user interacts with the product excessively because its design exploits psychological vulnerabilities to foster compulsive behaviour. Currency confusion: the user is misled about spending because real money is converted into virtual currency that obscures the true cost.

## Why it matters

Deceptive patterns win short-term metrics (signups, conversions, revenue) at the cost of trust, and increasingly at legal risk. A top designer treats this list as a set of red lines and audits their own flows against it, especially around defaults, cancellation, consent, urgency, and pricing.

title: Intercom, Designing Features Using Job Stories (Jobs to Be Done)
text:
## Jobs to Be Done and job stories

Intercom's product design practice is built on Jobs to Be Done: people do not buy products, they hire them to make progress in a particular situation. The design artifact that captures this is the job story, which reframes what to build around causality, context, and motivation rather than around who the user is.

## The job story format

A job story follows the structure: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]. For example, in a car-loan product: when car salespeople and their customers interact via the product, customers want to feel they can trust the organization, process, and salesperson, so clients feel safe entering financial information. The situation frames the context and any anxieties; the motivation states the goal; the expected outcome states the progress the person is trying to make. Notice the format deliberately omits an implementation, which keeps the team focused on the problem, not a premature solution.

## Why personas fall short

Intercom argues that personas are imaginary customers defined by attributes that do not acknowledge causality. Demographics like age, sex, and race reveal nothing about why someone makes a choice. The illustration: a Snickers bar is bought to solve a thirty-second hunger, the product and situation explain the purchase, not the buyer's demographic profile. Designing to a persona can lead teams to invent needs that a fictional character would have rather than needs real behavior reveals.

## Why user stories fall short

User stories (as a [persona], I want to [action], so that [benefit]) have three problems in this view: they rely on personas, they couple implementation with motivations and outcomes, and they ignore context, situations, and anxieties. When a feature fails, the coupling makes diagnosis impossible: you cannot tell whether the implementation was flawed or the motivational assumption was wrong.

## Designing around causality

Job stories succeed by observing how real people solve a problem now, exploring the context of the situation they are in, and then understanding causality, anxieties, and motivations. Grounding design in observable behavior and emotional drivers, rather than abstract attributes, lets teams craft solutions that fit the moment of use. The practical payoff for a product designer is a shared, testable statement of the problem that every design decision can be checked against.

title: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, Accessibility Principles (POUR)
text:
## The four principles of accessible design: POUR

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) from the W3C organize accessibility around four principles, abbreviated POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust. A product designer treats these as design constraints from the first sketch, not as a QA checklist bolted on at the end, because most accessibility failures are baked in by design decisions about color, layout, interaction, and content.

## Perceivable

Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. This requires text alternatives for non-text content (short equivalents for images, icons, buttons, and graphics, and descriptions for charts, diagrams, audio, and video); alternatives for time-based media such as transcripts and captions for audio and audio descriptions for video; adaptable content whose structure survives resizing and customization, with headings, lists, and tables properly marked up; and distinguishable content, meaning color is not used as the only way of conveying information, there is sufficient contrast between foreground and background, and text remains readable when enlarged up to 400 percent.

## Operable

User interface components and navigation must be operable. All functionality available by mouse must also be available by keyboard, with no keyboard traps. Users must have enough time and be able to stop, extend, or adjust time limits and control moving or blinking content. Content must not flash in ways that can cause seizures. Navigation and wayfinding must be clear: pages have descriptive titles and section headings, and there are multiple ways to find content. Alternative input modalities are supported, so gestures have non-dexterous alternatives and components avoid accidental activation.

## Understandable

Information and the operation of the user interface must be understandable. Text must be readable, which includes identifying the primary language of the page, defining unusual words, and using the clearest and simplest language possible. Operation must be predictable, so navigation repeated across pages appears in the same place and components have consistent labels. Input assistance must help users avoid and correct mistakes, with descriptive instructions, clear error messages, and suggestions for correction.

## Robust

Content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies. This means valid, well-structured markup, and providing a name, role, and value for any non-standard user interface components so screen readers and other tools can process them. Designing to POUR from the start is both an ethical baseline and, in many jurisdictions, a legal requirement.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, The False-Consensus Effect (You Are Not the User)
text:
## You are not the user: the false-consensus effect

The false-consensus effect refers to people's tendency to assume that others share their beliefs and will behave similarly in a given context. It is one of the most damaging anti-patterns in product design because it feels like insight when it is really projection. The effect was first documented in 1977 by Ross, Greene, and House in research on social perception and attribution.

## Why designers fall into it

Designers, developers, and researchers incorrectly project their own behaviors onto users because they have limited reference points. When professionals test interfaces primarily with themselves and their colleagues, they generalize from a narrow, unrepresentative sample. We naturally assume users resemble us, sharing our background, experiences, mental models, and technical proficiency, when in reality actual users are typically very different from those who build the product. This is reinforced by availability bias, the tendency to generalize from the examples most easily brought to mind.

## The core danger

The false-consensus effect causes teams to underestimate user confusion. The internal narrative becomes only someone who is stupid or very different from us could fail to figure this out, which is a dangerous assumption that leads to shipping designs that real people cannot use. Designers who fall for it dismiss usability problems as edge cases.

## The antidote

The cure is empirical validation: test with real users, not your colleagues. Rather than reasoning from your own reaction, study how actual target users respond to the design, and accept that different contexts and user populations behave differently than the design team expects. The professional discipline is to treat your own intuition as a hypothesis to be tested, never as evidence.

title: Kerry Rodden, The HEART Framework for UX Metrics
text:
## Measuring design impact: the HEART framework

The HEART framework is a way to measure the quality of the user experience at scale, developed at Google in 2010 by Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson, and Xin Fu, and published in the ACM CHI paper Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications. It gives product designers a vocabulary for connecting design work to measurable outcomes, which is essential for arguing the value of design beyond opinion.

## The five categories

Happiness measures user attitudes and satisfaction, typically through surveys, ratings, or in-app feedback (for example a satisfaction score or Net Promoter). Engagement measures the depth and frequency of interaction, how often and how deeply users use the product, focusing on meaningful actions rather than raw time-on-site. Adoption tracks new users and how quickly they take up a product or a new feature. Retention measures whether users keep coming back over time and is one of the strongest indicators of long-term value. Task success measures how effectively users complete key tasks, covering efficiency (speed), effectiveness (completion rate), and error rate.

## Goals, Signals, Metrics

HEART is paired with the Goals-Signals-Metrics (GSM) process, which keeps measurement focused. First, articulate the Goals of the product or feature (what success means for users and for the business). Second, identify the Signals, the observable user behaviors or attitudes that indicate progress toward those goals. Third, define the Metrics, the specific quantities you will track over time on a dashboard. Working top-down from goals prevents the common mistake of tracking whatever is easy to measure rather than what matters.

## Choosing categories

A key discipline is that you do not use every category for every project. You pick the HEART categories that map to your specific goal: a new feature launch usually emphasizes Adoption and Task Success; a retention initiative emphasizes Retention and Happiness; a redesign of a complex flow emphasizes Happiness and Task Success. HEART turns fuzzy claims about a better experience into a small set of tracked numbers tied to explicit goals.

title: Dubberly Design Office, Alan Cooper and the Goal-Directed Design Process
text:
## Goal-Directed Design and interaction design

Alan Cooper, author of About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design and The Inmates Are Running the Asylum, pioneered Goal-Directed Design and the use of personas as practical interaction-design tools. His central argument is that software should be designed from user goals first, and that this design work must be separated from and precede programming: design first, program second.

## Goals are not tasks

The foundational distinction is between goals and tasks. A goal is an end condition, whereas a task is an intermediate process needed to achieve the goal. As Cooper puts it, the goal is a steady thing, the tasks are transient. Goals endure while technology and workflows change, so designing to goals (why the person is here) rather than to tasks (the current steps) produces products that fit real human intent. Designers identify the correct tasks by working backward from goals instead of assuming today's steps are what the user actually wants.

## Personas and scenarios

Personas are composite portraits of a single, idealized user, given a name, a picture, a job description, specific goals, and a representative quote. Cooper calls personas the single most powerful design tool we use and the foundation for all subsequent goal-directed design. Distributing persona printouts in meetings keeps the team focused on a specific, named user rather than a vague elastic end user that designers unconsciously stretch to fit their own assumptions. Scenarios then describe how a persona uses the product to reach a goal, providing a narrative context in which to evaluate design decisions.

## The process and its philosophy

Goal-Directed Design runs from user research, through modeling users as personas, to defining requirements from persona goals and scenarios, to defining an interaction framework, and finally to refinement of the detailed design. Cooper advocates an organizational change to support this: pairing a designer with a design communicator in a two-person team, resembling the art director and copywriter model in advertising, so that design is collaborative and the responsibility for product quality and user satisfaction sits with designers rather than defaulting to programmers.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, The Aesthetic-Usability Effect
text:
## The aesthetic-usability effect

The aesthetic-usability effect is the tendency for users to perceive attractive products as more usable. People believe that designs that look better will work better, regardless of whether they actually do. For a product designer this cuts two ways: good aesthetics genuinely help, but they can also mask real usability problems and mislead a team about how well a design performs.

## Origin

In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaoru Kashimura of the Hitachi Design Center tested 26 variations of an ATM interface with 252 participants. They found that the correlation between participants' ratings of aesthetic appeal and perceived ease of use was stronger than the correlation between aesthetic appeal and actual ease of use. In other words, beauty influenced how usable people thought the interface was more than how usable it really was.

## Why it is a double-edged sword

When an interface looks attractive, users become more tolerant of minor usability issues. That tolerance is real and can build goodwill, but during user testing it can obscure genuine flaws, because a positive emotional response leads participants to overlook or forgive problems they would otherwise report. A design team can be lulled into thinking a flow works when the polish is simply covering for it. The effect has limits: a beautiful design cannot compensate for severe usability problems, and sacrificing function for appearance backfires.

## Design implications

Form and function should work together. Aesthetics deliver the most value when they support and enhance content and functionality rather than competing with them. The professional caution is to not let visual appeal substitute for usability evidence: keep testing for task success even when a design is beautiful, and never trade away core usability or accessibility for looks. Attractive visuals are a worthwhile investment, but they must not become a way to hide that the underlying interaction does not work.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Design Systems 101
text:
## What a design system is

A design system is a complete set of standards intended to manage design at scale using reusable components and patterns. It is more than a UI kit: it is the single source of truth that unites the visual language, the reusable building blocks, and the rules and processes for using them, so that many people across many products can build consistent experiences quickly.

## Style guide

A style guide provides specific implementation guidelines, visual references, and design principles for creating interfaces. It covers branding elements such as colors, typography, and logos; content guidance such as tone of voice; and interaction-design standards. The style guide encodes the design language, the shared set of decisions that give a product family its recognizable, coherent character.

## Component library and pattern library

A component library (also called a design library) houses predetermined, reusable UI elements, and for each element it typically documents the name, a description, customizable attributes, state variations, code snippets, and the implementation framework. A pattern library showcases collections of grouped UI elements, layouts, and templates meant to be reused and adapted. The two terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but they differ: components are individual UI elements, while patterns are groupings or layouts that combine multiple components to solve a recurring design problem.

## Benefits

A design system enables rapid replication and scaling of design, frees design resources to focus on complex problems rather than re-tweaking basic UI, establishes a unified language across cross-functional teams, ensures visual consistency across products and departments, and serves as an educational resource for junior designers who can learn the house style from the system.

## When to invest

Design systems are not free: they require dedicated teams for continuous maintenance and governance. They should be adopted when an organization anticipates years of replicable design work ahead. For a small one-off project, a full system is overkill; for a growing product family, it is what keeps quality and speed from degrading as the surface area expands. Governance, deciding who can add or change components and how, is what separates a living design system from a stale asset dump.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Progressive Disclosure
text:
## Progressive disclosure

Progressive disclosure is an interaction-design technique that resolves the tension between users' desire for both power and simplicity. Initially, show users only a few of the most important options, and offer a larger set of specialized options upon request. Advanced or rarely used features are deferred to a secondary screen or panel, revealed only when the user explicitly asks for them, so most people can finish common tasks without confronting unnecessary complexity.

## Usability benefits

Progressive disclosure improves three of the five usability components: learnability, efficiency, and error reduction. For novice users, showing only the core features helps prioritize their attention and helps them avoid mistakes. Advanced users benefit too, because they are not forced to scan long lists of features to find the common ones. Research indicates that users develop better mental models of a product when features are appropriately prioritized rather than dumped on screen all at once.

## Two design requirements

Success depends on two things. First, the correct feature split: the truly core features must appear in the initial, primary display, and only secondary items should be deferred; if you hide something people need often, you have hurt them, and if the first screen is still overwhelming you have gained nothing. Second, clear progression mechanics: the control that reveals the additional features must be obvious and well labeled, with strong information scent, so users understand what they will get when they open it and can predict where to find advanced options.

## Staged disclosure

Staged disclosure is a related variant that presents features sequentially across the steps of a task rather than hierarchically on one screen. Wizards are the classic example, walking a user through a multistep flow one decision at a time. Staged disclosure works best when the task steps are relatively independent; it struggles when steps require frequent back-and-forth navigation, because moving between stages then becomes costly. Progressive disclosure is one of the most reliable tools a product designer has for taming complexity without removing capability.

title: Jared Spool, The $300 Million Button
text:
## The $300 million button (an anti-pattern in problem framing)

Jared Spool's case study is a canonical lesson in how a small design decision, rooted in a wrong assumption, can cost a fortune, and how reframing the real problem unlocks huge value. A major ecommerce retailer required customers to register before they could buy. The checkout form was simple: two fields (email address, password), two buttons (Login and Register), and one Forgot Password link. The team assumed forcing registration was a minor step that would help returning customers check out faster.

## Why users failed

First-time buyers resented the mandatory registration. As one shopper put it, I'm not here to enter into a relationship, I just want to buy something. Repeat customers could not remember which email or password they had used; the company discovered that 45 percent of customers had multiple registrations in the system, some with up to 10 different accounts. The site was generating about 160,000 password-reset requests per day, and 75 percent of those users never completed their purchase after requesting a reset. The registration form, meant to help, was actively blocking sales.

## The fix

The designers changed almost nothing visually: they replaced the Register button with a Continue button and added a short message: you do not need to create an account to make purchases on our site. Simply click Continue to proceed to checkout. To make your future purchases even faster, you can create an account during checkout. This enabled guest checkout with optional account creation after the purchase.

## Results and the lesson

The number of customers purchasing increased by 45 percent, which produced an extra 15 million dollars in the first month and 300 million dollars in the first year. The lesson is that organizational assumptions about user behavior can silently create friction: the team assumed shoppers would not mind registering for future convenience, but observing real users revealed the opposite, that they prioritized completing the immediate transaction over building a relationship. A top product designer treats every assumption baked into a flow as a hypothesis to test, and reframes the problem from what the business wants users to do to what users are actually trying to accomplish.

title: Bill Buxton, Sketching User Experiences (summary of Getting the Design Right and the Right Design)
text:
## Sketch versus prototype

In Sketching User Experiences: Getting the Design Right and the Right Design, Bill Buxton draws a sharp distinction between sketches and prototypes. Sketches are quick, cheap, disposable, and deliberately unfinished; their job is to suggest and to ask questions, to externalize a lot of ideas fast so they can be compared and discarded. Prototypes are more developed and more committed; their job is to describe and to answer questions about a chosen solution. Confusing the two, treating an early exploration as a thing to refine, kills the exploration. Sketches pose questions, prototypes provide answers.

## Getting the right design versus getting the design right

Buxton's central idea is a two-phase view of design. Getting the right design is divergent: generating multiple, meaningfully distinct alternative solutions before committing to any direction. Getting the design right is convergent: refining and perfecting the chosen solution through iteration. Both matter, but teams routinely skip the divergent phase and jump straight to polishing the first idea. Buxton's warning is blunt: unless you came up with a number of meaningfully distinct alternative solutions, you have no idea how good the solution you converged upon actually was. Committing early to a single concept, without alternatives to judge it against, is a core product-design failure.

## The design funnel and why alternatives matter

Design proceeds like a funnel: it starts wide, with broad exploration and many rough ideas, and narrows as concepts are refined and validated, pulling in input from design, engineering, management, marketing, and sales as it goes. Because ideas are comparatively cheap, generating several divergent sketch alternatives early lets a team compare options before spending money and time on development. This is a discipline achievable on budget and schedule: the cost of many sketches is trivial next to the cost of building the wrong thing well. The practical lesson for a product designer is to protect a genuine divergence phase, produce and show real alternatives, and resist the pull to fall in love with the first plausible solution.

title: Figma, The Designer's Handbook for Developer Handoff
text:
## Handoff as ongoing collaboration

Figma frames developer handoff not as a single throw-it-over-the-wall moment but as ongoing collaboration. Design is what we want and development is essentially what we have, and the job of handoff is to close that gap continuously rather than once. Bringing engineers in early, even at wireframe stage for a feasibility gut check, prevents expensive surprises later.

## Prepare the file

Good handoff starts with a clean, legible file. Use descriptive, semantic layer names rather than default ones, remove unnecessary layers that only confuse developers, and pre-configure export settings for assets with documented specifications. A tidy file communicates intent and reduces the questions a developer has to ask.

## Lean on the design system

Use existing components, styles, and variables (design tokens) consistently so that what the developer builds maps to shared, named decisions rather than one-off values. Features like code syntax and Code Connect bridge design-friendly names to implementation details, keeping design and code in sync. When you deviate from an established pattern, document the reasoning so the deviation is a decision, not an accident.

## Anticipate implementation reality

Design for responsive behavior across breakpoints, not just fixed frame sizes, and account for edge cases such as text wrapping, truncation, and user font-size preferences. Think about how layout compounds under responsive calculation. Designing these states up front means the developer is not left guessing what happens when content is longer or the viewport is smaller.

## Annotate, share language, and build in accessibility

In Dev Mode, add explicit annotations specifying spacing, whether a value is fixed or responsive, and where assets live, with dedicated annotation categories for layout and accessibility. Develop a shared language: distinguish links from buttons by function rather than appearance, and document how text styles map to semantic HTML hierarchy, which affects both accessibility and page structure. Integrate accessibility early, contrast checking, semantic HTML implications, and tab order, treating these not as limitations but as opportunities to clarify design intent. Mark designs Ready for Dev before sharing Dev Mode links to signal finalization, then stay available for questions and use comment threads for asynchronous follow-up.

title: 37signals, Getting Real: Make Opinionated Software (reproduced chapter)
text:
## Opinionated design: your product should take sides

In the Getting Real chapter Make Opinionated Software, 37signals argues against the common belief that a product should be neutral and maximally flexible. Some people argue software should be agnostic, and they call that view wrong. Their position: the best software has a vision, the best software takes sides. A product that tries to be everything to everyone, endlessly configurable and opinion-free, ends up being nothing in particular to anyone.

## Users want an approach, not just features

When someone uses software, they are not just looking for features, they are looking for an approach, a vision. People are drawn to products with a clear point of view about how a problem should be solved. The practical instruction is direct: decide what your vision is and run with it. A confident, opinionated design gives users a coherent mental model and a reason to prefer it over a feature-matched but characterless competitor.

## Decide the little details so customers do not have to

A key move of opinionated design is to make decisions on the user's behalf rather than offloading them as preferences. Offering endless options and settings is described as the easy way out: it looks flexible but actually pushes the hard design work onto the user. Instead, decide the little details so your customers do not have to. Say no to most feature requests and build only what is essential to the vision. Every preference you avoid adding is a decision you made for the user, and a simpler product for them.

## The tension with data-driven design

Opinionated design sits in deliberate tension with a purely data-driven approach that tries to A/B test every pixel and defers all judgment to metrics. The Getting Real stance is that taste, vision, and a strong point of view are legitimate and necessary design inputs, and that a product built entirely by committee and experiment, with no one willing to take a side, tends toward a bland local optimum. A mature product designer uses data to inform and to catch mistakes, but still brings judgment and a coherent point of view rather than abdicating design decisions to the test results.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Storyboards Help Visualize UX Ideas
text:
## Storyboards in product design

A storyboard is a storytelling tool that communicates a story through images displayed in a sequence of panels that chronologically maps the story's main events. It borrows directly from film, animation, and comic books, adapted for design to provide a visual narrative of a user's experience over time. For a product designer, a storyboard turns an abstract flow or scenario into a concrete, human sequence that a whole team can react to.

## The three core components

A storyboard has three parts. The scenario grounds the storyboard in a specific user story, naming the persona and giving a brief description, for example corporate buyer James needs to replenish office supplies. The visuals are the sequential images, one per step, ranging from low-fidelity sketches to high-fidelity illustrations or photos; they depict the user's environment, emotional state, device interactions, and context. The captions are concise text accompanying each visual, typically no more than two bullet points, describing the user's actions, environment, emotions, and device.

## Why storyboards work

Storyboards capture attention and enable empathy. By visualizing actual user interactions, including quotes, body language, and environmental factors, they help teams and stakeholders quickly and memorably grasp the context a design must serve, in a way plain text descriptions cannot. They foster shared understanding and create common ground across a cross-functional team, which is valuable because much of a designer's job is aligning people on the same picture of the user.

## When to use them

Storyboards are useful for distilling usability-testing findings into a shareable narrative, for enriching journey maps with contextual imagery, for establishing prioritization by making user pain points vivid, and for exploring ideated scenarios during conceptual phases. They are deliberately about the whole context of use, the before and after around a screen, not just the interface, which is what makes them a product-design tool rather than only an interface tool. Storyboarding keeps the team designing for a real moment in a real person's day rather than for an isolated screen.

title: Daniel Zacarias (Folding Burritos), The Complete Guide to the Kano Model
text:
## The Kano model: deciding what to design

The Kano model helps a product designer decide which features actually move satisfaction, by classifying features against two axes: a satisfaction axis (from frustration to delight) and a functionality axis (from no implementation to optimal implementation). The relationship between how much you invest in a feature and how satisfied customers feel is different for each category, producing non-linear satisfaction curves.

## The feature categories

Must-be (basic) features are expected; they prevent dissatisfaction but do not create satisfaction. We need to have them, but having them will not make customers more satisfied, for example a phone that can make calls or a hotel that has beds. Even large investment never pushes satisfaction into the positive range; their absence causes strong dissatisfaction. Performance (one-dimensional) features have a linear relationship: the more we provide, the more satisfied customers become, for example battery life, gas mileage, or storage space. Attractive (delighters or exciters) features are unexpected and produce outsized positive reactions even at modest functionality, for example the original iPhone touchscreen that blew people away; beyond a point they show diminishing returns. Indifferent features produce no meaningful reaction whether present or absent, making them essentially money sinks to avoid. Reverse features are ones customers actively dislike having and prefer absent, signaling a misread of what customers want.

## The natural decay of delight

A critical temporal dynamic is that attractive features turn into performance and then must-be features as time goes by. The iPhone's revolutionary touchscreen became a basic expectation that every phone must have. This disenchantment results from technological evolution and competitors catching up, which means any Kano analysis is just a photograph reflecting that moment's reality and must be repeated over time. Today's delighter is tomorrow's table stakes.

## Prioritization

The recommended sequence is to secure Must-be features first (you cannot compete without them), then invest in Performance features (where more is measurably better and you can differentiate), then add a small number of Attractive features (to delight and stand out), and avoid Indifferent and Reverse features entirely. For a product designer, Kano is a discipline against two failure modes: neglecting basics while chasing flashy delighters, and pouring effort into features customers are indifferent to.
